beats.narration_text: Hej — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. Chapter two ended on a requirement: hand the model the right text, chosen for the question being asked. 'Right' means 'about the same thing' — but a computer can't just read and tell. This chapter builds the one idea that makes that comparison possible: turning text into numbers.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath: turn every piece of text into a list of numbers — a vector — learned so that similar meanings end up as similar numbers. Then comparing meaning becomes comparing distance. That's an embedding, and it's the foundation the rest of this book stands on.

beats.narration_text: Word2vec started this: a network trained over one point six billion words learns, for every word, a few hundred numbers — not hand-assigned, discovered purely from which words appear near which other words. Words used in similar contexts land with similar vectors.

beats.narration_text: A famous demonstration of how much structure these vectors capture: king, minus man, plus woman, lands close to queen. Hold this loosely — later replication work found this specific result depends on excluding the query word itself from the search; skip that step, and the closest vector to the equation is often just 'king' again.

'queen' settles in terracotta
caveat line fades in: depends on excluding the query word from the search

props.caveat: Depends on excluding the query word from the search — without that step, the closest vector is often just "king" again (Mikolov, Yih & Zweig, 2013; later replication work).

beats.narration_text: Word2vec works word by word — a clean first example, but not what RAG actually embeds. A help-desk question is a whole passage. BERT learns deep contextual representations, but its raw output compares whole sentences poorly. Sentence-BERT restructures it so one vector stands for one whole passage, meaningfully comparable to another.

beats.narration_text: And the gain isn't just cleaner comparisons — it's speed. Finding the most similar pair among ten thousand sentences took roughly sixty-five hours with raw BERT. Restructured as Sentence-BERT, the same task, at comparable accuracy, takes about five seconds.

beats.narration_text: Once text is a vector, comparing meaning becomes geometry: how close are two vectors? The standard measure is cosine similarity — the angle between them — and it's older than embeddings themselves, borrowed straight from classical information retrieval.

passage vector draws in terracotta
angle arc draws between them
caption settles with citation

props.headline: Closeness, Measured
props.caption: cosine similarity — the angle between two vectors (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, 2008)
props.sparkLine: An old tool. A richer vector.

beats.narration_text: Here's the payoff. Before embeddings, comparing text meant comparing literal words. That fails constantly — people ask about the same thing in completely different words. Embeddings compare what the text is about, not its characters. The question doesn't need the manual's exact wording — it only needs to land near it.

beats.narration_text: 'How much vacation do I get' and 'what's the PTO policy' share almost no words — and land close together, because they're the same request. 'How do I request time off' and 'how do I request a new laptop' share the exact phrase 'how do I request' — and land far apart, because they're not the same request at all.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. Text becomes a vector, learned so similar meanings land as similar numbers — word2vec proved the idea, Sentence-BERT made it work for whole passages, fast. Cosine similarity measures the closeness. And closeness in that space is a proxy for closeness in meaning — not perfect, but good enough that the rest of this book is built on it.

artifactLines: Text becomes a vector — learned from patterns of usage, not hand-assigned (Mikolov et al., 2013).
Word-level vectors aren't enough for RAG — Sentence-BERT makes whole-passage comparison both accurate and fast (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019).
Cosine similarity — the angle between two vectors — measures that closeness, a tool older than embeddings themselves (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, 2008).
Closeness in the vector space is a proxy for closeness in meaning: imperfect, but the foundation the rest of this book depends on.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Take three short phrases I'll give you, and reason — without running any actual computation — about which two are most likely to land closest together in embedding space, and why. Then take one pair that shares a lot of words but means different things, and explain why they should land far apart anyway.' Bring your own three phrases, and check whether your intuition about meaning actually matches what a real embedding model would place close together.
